newsitem.title: USA: Rich, newly rich nations set out anti-crisis plan.
newsitem.headline: Rich, newly rich nations set out anti-crisis plan.

text.p: By Rich Miller, U.S. Economics Correspondent
An unusual alliance of industrial nations and rapidly developing countries proposed a wide-ranging strategy on Tuesday for reducing the risk of financial turbulence in emerging markets.

The plan, unveiled on the final day of the semi-annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, sets out guidelines for strengthening banking and financial systems in emerging markets and ways to implement them.

The aim of the exercise is to try to prevent the kind of financial crises that rocked Mexico in 1994/95 and sparked an armed revolt in Albania this year after the collapse of a string of fraudulent, unregulated pyramid investment schemes there.

"People are dying in Albania and security forces are being mobilised in no small part because of the failure of regulation," U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers told reporters at a briefing on the new strategy.

The broad-based regulatory guidelines, which were drawn up by a working group of experts headed by Italian Treasury Ministry Director General Mario Draghi, cover everything from accounting standards to insurance supervision.

Among the measures suggested: passage of a bankruptcy code, timely publication of financial data by banks and other institutions, establishment of adequate capital requirements and a supervisory structure free from political interference.

The guidelines will not be mandatory, but may be used by the IMF and World Bank in structuring their loan programmes and advice for emerging market economies and by international investors in deciding where to put their money.

Experts from eight industrial countries -- Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, Sweden and the United States -- and eight emerging markets -- Argentina, Hong Kong, Indonesia, South Korea, Mexico, Poland, Singapore and Thailand -- drew up the report on financial stability. It was shared with the rest of the IMF's over 180 nations on Tuesday.
Summers said the initiative grew out of the realisation that financial crises result from both the failure of broad economic policies and from inadequate supervision of banks and other institutions.

He pinpointed two problems that frequently beset financial systems in emerging economies -- "related lending" by banks and other institutions that grant credit at favourable terms to insiders and the lack of a "national culture of credit" that mandates the repayment of loans.

Morris Goldstein, of the Institute for International Economics think tank, estimates that three-fourths of the world's economies have been hit by banking crises over the past 15 years. Developing nations alone have spent almost $250 billion bailing out their banks.

According to the report released on Tuesday, financial turbulence can be touched off by a variety of factors -- from a sudden, sharp drop in inflation that hurts property prices to liberalisation of inadequately-supervised markets.

To help counteract that, the working party headed by Draghi recommended the pursuit of sound economic policies and creation of "robust" financial systems that are adequately supervised, but not overly so.
Draghi told reporters that the primary responsibility for making the plan work rested with the individual countries and their regulators. But it would be up to the IMF to oversee that.
"It is the IMF who should blow the whistle" if countries do not comply, Draghi said.

But Argentine Finance Secretary Pablo Guidotti, who was also a member of the working group, said the discipline for the plan would ultimately be provided by the financial markets, as global investors decided where to put their money.
